The `wiki_place_page` tool returned a generic guide for every call at both the county and state level — these are not Cook County or Illinois-specific pages. I have solid grounding from `collections_search`, `volume_search`, the `wiki_search` results (which returned Illinois Vital Records content with source URLs), and the Wikipedia Great Chicago Fire entries. I'll now compile the guide from verified tool output.

---

# Locality Guide: Cook County (Chicago), Illinois (1860–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Cook County was established in 1831; Chicago was incorporated as a city in 1837.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois (state)
- **Population during period:** Cook County's population was rapidly expanding through this era — Chicago grew from roughly 109,000 in 1860 to over 300,000 by 1880, a pace driven almost entirely by immigrant labor. No numerical figure was returned by the `place_population` tool for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Meatpacking, lumber, grain trade, manufacturing, and railroad hub. Lake Michigan port commerce was central. The Great Fire obliterated the central business district but rebuilding was swift and massive.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, Scandinavian (Swedish, Norwegian), and Bohemian (Czech) immigrant communities, with smaller Polish, Italian, and African American populations. Chain migration was strong — ethnic enclaves created parallel institutional records.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Irish and German parishes, with separate national parishes for each ethnic group), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian), Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, Jewish, and Bohemian evangelical congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, and left more than 100,000 homeless. The Cook County Courthouse burned completely, destroying the county's civil vital records, deed books, court records, and tax rolls. ([Wikipedia: Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire))

## Boundary changes

Cook County's boundaries were stable throughout the target period (1860–1885). No subdivisions or boundary changes affected which jurisdiction held records during this window. The county encompassed Chicago and surrounding townships throughout.

**Critical split: before and after October 10, 1871.** The fire acts as a hard line in the record landscape. Civil vital records, county court records, deed books, and tax rolls filed at the Cook County Courthouse before October 1871 are destroyed. Records created after that date survive and are increasingly available. This is a temporal split — the rule is clean: any record filed at the Courthouse before the fire is presumed lost; check substitute sources. Any record filed after reconstruction is present.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Cook County local level, births and deaths:** Local registration in Cook County began in 1871, per the FamilySearch Wiki Illinois Vital Records page ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration)). The earliest surviving registration begins with the post-fire re-establishment. Most pre-October 1871 Cook County vital records were destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire.
- **Statewide level:** Illinois did not require statewide vital registration until 1916 (with compliance improving through the 1920s), per the same FamilySearch Wiki source. For births and deaths before 1916, researchers must use substitute sources.
- **What exists on FamilySearch (indexed collections):**
  - "Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940" — 1,450,000 records (collection ID 2024189)
  - "Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947" — 980,000 records (collection ID 1913456)
  - "Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920" — 620,000 records (collection ID 1756321)
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images for all three collections on FamilySearch.
- **Gaps:** All pre-October 1871 civil vital records are destroyed. The 1871 starting date on these collections reflects the post-fire restart of registration, not original records from that year.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the primary substitute (see below).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Irish, German, Bohemian, and Polish national parishes), German Lutheran, Scandinavian Lutheran, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist, Jewish congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. These are the single most important source for pre-1871 vital events in Chicago. National parishes kept records in the heritage language of the congregation.
- **Where held:** Many surviving registers are held by individual parishes, diocesan archives (Catholic: Archdiocese of Chicago Archives), Lutheran synodal archives, and some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" — 285,000 records (collection ID 1803978). This spans the entire period and is the most important pre-fire resource on FamilySearch. Indexed + images.
- **Language:** German-language registers are common for German Catholic, German Lutheran, and Bohemian congregations. Irish Catholic registers are in English. Swedish and Norwegian Lutheran registers are in those languages.
- **Key point:** Many church registers were kept at the parish, not the courthouse, and therefore survived the fire. A family documented only in a church register before 1871 has recoverable evidence even when civil records are gone.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1885 schedules all cover Cook County and are available. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed (separate fire at the National Archives, 1921) — Cook County is no better off than anywhere else for 1890. The 1870 census, taken just before the fire, captures the Chicago population at its pre-fire peak and is a critical source.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules list deaths in the year preceding each census. These are a critical substitute for destroyed death records, particularly for the period around the fire.
- **State census:** Illinois took a state census in 1865, which falls squarely between the 1860 and 1870 federal censuses. The Illinois State Archives in Springfield holds state census fragments; availability varies by county and township.
- **Access:** Federal census schedules are indexed + images on both FamilySearch and Ancestry. Mortality schedules are available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records

- **Pre-fire (before October 1871):** Cook County probate files and circuit court records held at the Courthouse are destroyed. Per the Wikipedia Great Chicago Fire entry, the Courthouse's destruction took court records and all that was filed there.
- **Post-fire (October 1871 onward):** Probate and court records resume and survive. The Cook County Circuit Court held probate matters at the county level.
- **Naturalization:** Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records survive from the 1840s onward, per the FamilySearch Wiki Illinois Vital Records page ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records)). These are among the most valuable surviving pre-fire documents naming Chicago immigrants. They establish arrival dates, origin countries, and sometimes birthdates.
- **Where held:** Cook County Circuit Court Clerk's office (originals); some are available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Digitization level:** Post-fire probate records — browse-only or microfilm for much of this period; naturalization records partially indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Illinois is a federal-land state — land was originally distributed by the federal government under the rectangular survey system. Original land patents are at the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office (GLO) website (glorecords.blm.gov), which is free and searchable.
- **Post-fire reconstruction:** After the fire, the Illinois legislature passed the Burnt Record Act of 1872, which required property owners to re-register their deeds. This created a specific post-fire series of property re-recordings. FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 009982111, 112 images, 41% indexed, covering 1871–1880) of post-fire property re-recordings.
- **Pre-fire deeds:** Lost at the Courthouse. The Chicago Title and Trust Company's insurance records became a vital substitute for establishing pre-fire property ownership, per the Wikipedia Great Chicago Fire entry.
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (post-fire originals); BLM GLO for original patents; Illinois State Archives for some pre-fire copies that were held elsewhere.
- **Digitization level:** Post-fire property records partially indexed (41%) on FamilySearch — browsable with partial name search capability. Pre-fire: destroyed, with insurance record substitutes held physically.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) falls directly before the target window. Many Chicago men served; the war ended 6 years before the fire, so veterans and their families were well-established in Chicago by 1871.
- **Record types:** Civil War service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are at the National Archives (NARA). These are held at the federal level and were not affected by the Chicago fire. Pension files are particularly valuable — they contain sworn statements of age, family relationships, marriage dates, and places of birth that substitute for destroyed civil vital records.
- **Draft registrations:** Civil War draft registration records (1863 and 1865) cover Cook County and are indexed on Ancestry and Fold3.
- **State records:** Illinois adjutant general records are at the Illinois State Archives in Springfield.
- **Digitization level:** NARA Civil War pension files are indexed on Ancestry and Fold3 (subscription). Service records are indexed + images on Fold3.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (non-sectarian, founded 1860), Rosehill Cemetery (non-sectarian, founded 1859), St. Boniface Cemetery (German Catholic), Calvary Cemetery (Catholic, Evanston). These were outside the burn zone and their sexton records survived.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has significant Cook County coverage. BillionGraves also covers many Chicago cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records at individual cemeteries. Graceland and Rosehill are well-documented and some records have been transcribed by genealogical societies.
- **Digitization level:** Cemetery headstone databases (Find A Grave, BillionGraves) are free and indexed. Original sexton records are physical-only at the respective cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune (founded 1847) is the dominant surviving paper and is available on Newspapers.com and ProQuest Historical Newspapers. The Chicago Times and other papers also published in this period.
- **Critical value for this period:** Newspapers are one of the most underused but richest substitutes for the fire era. The Tribune published lists of fire victims, displaced families, relief committee rolls, and property loss notices within days of the fire. Marriage and death notices in newspapers often pre-date or substitute for missing civil registration.
- **Where held:** Chicago Tribune digitized archives on ProQuest and Newspapers.com; the Newberry Library and Chicago History Museum hold microfilm runs of many Chicago newspapers.
- **Digitization level:** Newspapers.com covers the Chicago Tribune and other papers in a name-searchable format (subscription). ProQuest Historical Newspapers has full-text search (subscription, often free via public library). Microfilm browse-only for papers not yet digitized.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Chicago immigrants primarily arrived through New York (Castle Garden, then Ellis Island from 1892), Baltimore, Boston, New Orleans, and Quebec. Chicago itself is an inland city — there are no Chicago port-of-entry records. Records were generated at the port of arrival, not in Chicago.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (at NARA, indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch), declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed at Chicago courts — survived the fire for post-1871 filings; pre-1871 Cook County naturalizations in Circuit and Superior Courts survive from the 1840s per the FamilySearch Wiki).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and young children. Always examine the full manifest for the entire family, not just the head of household. Pre-1895 lists are typically shorter (name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin); post-1895 lists (and especially after 1906) carry much more detail including nearest relative in country of origin and U.S. contact.
- **Access:** Ancestry and FamilySearch both index passenger lists. Naturalization records filed at Cook County courts are at the Cook County Circuit Court Clerk's office; many are indexed on Ancestry.

### Tax records

- **Pre-fire:** Cook County tax rolls held at the Courthouse are destroyed.
- **Post-fire:** Tax records resume in 1871–1872. Illinois State Archives holds some state-level tax records.
- **Substitute value:** The 1860 and 1870 federal census non-population schedules (agricultural, manufacturing, mortality) can substitute for missing tax records and document a family's economic position before the fire.

### Other record types

- **City directories:** Chicago city directories were published from 1839 and continued without interruption through and after the fire. They are one of the most powerful tools for this period — placing a person at a specific address and occupation in years between censuses and immediately before/after the fire. The Newberry Library holds an extensive run. Many are digitized and searchable through Ancestry.
- **Fire relief records:** After the Great Fire, the Chicago Relief and Aid Society distributed relief to displaced families and kept detailed records of who applied, what they received, and where they were relocated. These records are held at the Chicago History Museum and name thousands of families displaced by the fire. This is a direct and specific source for fire-affected families that most researchers overlook.
- **Coroner's records:** Cook County Coroner inquests survive from the 1870s onward. For deaths that attracted an inquest (accidents, fires, suspicious circumstances), the inquest file names witnesses, relatives, and circumstances and often substitutes for a missing death record.
- **School records:** Chicago Board of Education records exist from the 1840s. Enrollment records can document a child's presence in the city during the period. Held at the Chicago Board of Education archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Cook County Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1.45M records, ID 2024189); Cook County Death Records 1871–1947 (980K records, ID 1913456); Cook County Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K records, ID 1756321); Cook County Church Records 1833–1925 (285K records, ID 1803978); 2 digitized volumes of pre/post-fire court and property records (browse-only and partially indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1860/1870/1880; Civil War draft registrations; pension files; passenger lists; city directories; Cook County naturalization records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records; pension files; draft registrations | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Chicago Tribune and other Chicago papers — obituaries, marriage notices, fire victim lists | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Illinois | Free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery headstone database for Cook County cemeteries | Free |

**October 8–10, 1871 — Great Chicago Fire:** The burning of the Cook County Courthouse destroyed:
- All Cook County civil vital records filed before the fire (births, marriages, deaths)
- County deed books and property records (land transfer history before 1871)
- Circuit Court and Superior Court records held at the Courthouse (civil cases, some naturalizations from those courts)
- Tax rolls

- Records held outside the Courthouse — church registers (kept at parishes), federal census schedules (held at Washington), federal court records, passenger lists, and military pension files were all unaffected.
- Cook County naturalization records in the Circuit Court and Superior Court survive from the 1840s onward per the FamilySearch Wiki — the filing location and survival status of specific pre-fire batches should be verified at the court clerk's office, but the FamilySearch Wiki specifically states these survive.
- City directories, which were private publications, survived.

**1921 — National Archives fire:** The Commerce Department building fire destroyed approximately 80% of the 1890 federal census for the entire United States. The 1885 Illinois state census (if it was taken; availability should be verified at the Illinois State Archives) and city directories from the late 1880s are the primary bridges between the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses for Cook County.

**Substitute sources for destroyed records:**

| Destroyed record | Best substitute |
|---|---|
| Pre-1871 civil birth records | Church baptismal registers; later delayed birth affidavits |
| Pre-1871 civil death records | Church burial registers; 1870 mortality schedule; newspaper obituaries; cemetery sexton records |
| Pre-1871 civil marriage records | Church marriage registers; newspaper marriage notices |
| Pre-1871 county deed books | Burnt Record Act 1872 re-registrations; Chicago Title & Trust insurance records; BLM GLO patents |
| Pre-1871 probate/court files | Newspaper legal notices (probate was published); post-fire re-filing of claims |
| 1890 federal census | 1880 + 1900 census; 1885/1895 state census (check Illinois State Archives); city directories 1888–1899; Veterans' schedules (GAR members) |

- **Start with the 1870 census.** The 1870 federal census was enumerated before the fire and is the last complete population snapshot of pre-fire Chicago. It captures names, ages, birthplaces, and household composition for families who would later be displaced. This is your anchor document. Mortality schedules from the same year cover deaths in 1869–1870.
- **The Chicago Relief and Aid Society records are specific to fire-affected families.** If your family was displaced, this is the only record type that directly documents the fire's effect on them as individuals. It is held at the Chicago History Museum and is not available online.
- **Treat church registers as the primary vital record source before 1871.** The key question is: what denomination was the family? Ethnic origin usually predicts denomination. A German Catholic family would appear in a German national parish register, not an Irish one. Identify the most likely parish by neighborhood and ethnic community, then search that parish's records specifically.
- **Use city directories to track movement.** Chicago directories, published annually, let you follow a family across years — establishing presence before the fire, disappearance at the time of the fire, and reappearance at a new address afterward. A family that vanishes from the 1871 directory and reappears at a different address in 1872 is likely fire-displaced.
- **Civil War pension files substitute for missing vital records.** A Union veteran's pension file (held at NARA, indexed on Ancestry/Fold3) contains sworn affidavits of the veteran's age, marriage date, wife's age, children's names and births, and places of origin. These are often more detailed than any civil vital record would have been. If a male ancestor was of service age (born roughly 1820–1847), always check for a pension file.
- **Naturalization records survive from the pre-fire period.** The FamilySearch Wiki states Cook County Circuit Court and Superior Court naturalization records survive from the 1840s ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records)). For immigrant families, a declaration of intention or certificate of naturalization establishes country of origin, sometimes port and date of arrival, and age — information destroyed in civil records.
- **Newspaper fire coverage is a genealogical source.** The Chicago Tribune and other papers published lists of the dead, the missing, known survivors, relief applicants, and property losses within days of the fire. Searching digitized newspaper archives for a surname in the weeks immediately following October 10, 1871 can yield a direct documentary mention of a fire-affected family.
- **The Burnt Record Act of 1872 created a searchable post-fire property record.** Families who re-registered their deeds under this act appear in a specific series of re-recordings, partially indexed (41%) on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 009982111). If property ownership is the research question, this is the starting point for establishing who held what after the fire.
- **Do not assume a record is gone simply because it isn't online.** The destroyed/online gap for pre-1871 Chicago is real, but the substitute landscape is rich. Many families can be reconstructed through the combination of church registers, city directories, 1870 census, naturalization records, and military pension files even when no civil vital records survive.

The fire burned the Cook County Courthouse and destroyed virtually all civil vital records, deed books, and court files that had been filed there before the disaster. The records that survive — and there are many — are the ones that were never stored at the Courthouse: church baptism, marriage, and burial registers (often kept in German, Swedish, or other immigrant languages); the 1870 federal census taken just months before the fire; city directories published every year without interruption; federal military pension files at the National Archives; and the Chicago Relief and Aid Society's register of displaced families, held at the Chicago History Museum and available only in person. The single most important caution is that "not found online" does not mean "does not exist" — Chicago's pre-fire substitute sources are rich but scattered across specialized repositories rather than a single database.

If you want to go further, the next step is building a research plan that sequences exactly which of these record types to search for your specific ancestor, in what order, at which repository.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formal period:** French Louisiana existed from 1682; effective settlement began ca. 1699. France ceded the western territory to Spain via the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), and the eastern portion to Britain. Spain administered the western colony until 1800, when it was retroceded to France; the United States acquired it in the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718), seat of the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (France), then Spanish Louisiana (1769-1800), then briefly French again before U.S. acquisition.
- **Population during period:** Population data for the colonial period was not returned by the tools. French censuses and census-like rolls survive and are described under Census Records.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar), fur trade, maritime commerce. Enslaved labor was central under the Code Noir.
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers (including Canadians and Acadians after 1755), African-origin enslaved people, Native American populations, German settlers (German Coast, 1720s), Spanish settlers (post-1769), and free people of color.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism exclusively (legally mandated under both French and Spanish rule).
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Natchez Massacre (1729); Acadian deportation and resettlement (1755-1785); Spanish takeover (1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary and jurisdictional changes
Three distinct administrations during the 1700s: French Louisiana (1699-1769), Spanish Louisiana (1769-1800), brief French interval (1800-1803). Records for a single family may span all three in the same parish registers and notarial archives. The effective split date for French vs. Spanish records is 1769, not 1762.

## Available record types

### Vital records
No civil registration existed during the French colonial period. Catholic sacramental registers are the functional vital records. St. Louis Cathedral registers survive from 1720. FamilySearch collection 1612905 covers 1718-1925 with ~987,654 records and 493,827 images.

### Church records
Roman Catholicism only. Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Records in French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769). Held at the Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, Louisiana Historical Center, and partially on FamilySearch. Two digitized volumes on FamilySearch (image groups 004330991 and 004330992) are browse-only, 0% indexed, in French and Spanish.

### Census records
French colonial recensements and Spanish colonial censuses exist but are largely at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France). Not available in an indexed online database. U.S. federal census begins 1810, post-colonial period.

### Probate and court records
FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984). Superior Council records (1699-1769) are at the Louisiana Historical Center, partially digitized as image group 004330992 (149 images, browse-only, French/Spanish). Spanish Cabildo records continue the series post-1769.

### Land records
French arpent-lot system along waterways. Concessions via Superior Council (French) and Cabildo (Spanish). American State Papers: Public Lands documents colonial grants confirmed post-Purchase. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial property records from 1730s onward.

### Notarial records
Central to Louisiana research due to civil law tradition. Contain wills, marriage settlements, property sales, manumissions, contracts. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access. Records from 1730s onward.

### Military records
French military records at Archives de la Guerre (Vincennes, France); Spanish military records at Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Archivo General de Simancas. No FamilySearch-indexed colonial Louisiana military collection identified.

### Cemetery records
Burials recorded in Catholic parish registers. St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 established 1789. FindAGrave (findagrave.com) available but colonial-era coverage sparse.

### Newspaper records
First Louisiana newspaper (Moniteur de la Louisiane) begun 1794. No newspapers existed for the French period (pre-1762).

### Immigration records
French colonial emigrant contracts and ship lists at ANOM (France). Acadian resettlement records in ANOM and published indexes. Slave manifests and Code Noir baptismal entries in sacramental registers.

### Tax records
Taille and tithe records embedded in Superior Council/Cabildo proceedings. Colonial census rolls partly function as property counts. Held at Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1718-1925 (col. 1612905); Probate Records 1756-1984 (col. 2078341); 2 browse-only digitized volumes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal-era records; some colonial-era materials | Free/request |
| Fold3 | Military records (general) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (sparse for colonial era) | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans) | Superior Council and Cabildo records; partially digitized | In-person; some online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s; oldest continuous notarial office in North America | In-person; finding aids online |
| Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans | Catholic parish registers | In-person; contact archdiocese |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | State-era and some colonial-era materials | In-person; online catalog |
| ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records; census rolls; emigrant records | In-person or written request; partial digitization at archim.culture.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records (1769-1803) | In-person or written request; partial digitization at pares.mcu.es |
| Tulane University (Howard-Tilton Library) | Louisiana Historical Association collection; colonial manuscripts | In-person; some online finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial census rolls (at ANOM)
- French military records (Archives de la Guerre, Vincennes)
- Spanish military and administrative records (Archivo General de Indias, Seville)
- Ship passenger and emigrant contracts (ANOM)
- Most Natchitoches-area and upper-territory records

## Known record losses
- St. Louis Cathedral early registers damaged; surviving registers begin ca. 1720
- Some Superior Council records lost or damaged during administration transfers (1769; 1800-1803)
- Mobile and eastern French Louisiana ceded to Britain 1763; those records are in British colonial archives or NARA, not New Orleans repositories

## Research tips
- Catholic parish is the genealogical jurisdiction, not any civil unit. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- All colonial records are in French or Spanish — browsing the unindexed volumes requires ability to read 18th-century French and Spanish script
- Notarial archives are essential for wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- Search both French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769) series for any family with records spanning 1769
- Code Noir entries in sacramental registers are the primary source for enslaved ancestors
- American State Papers: Public Lands documents colonial land grants confirmed post-Purchase
- Published genealogical literature (De Ville, Robichaux) contains transcriptions of hard-to-access colonial records

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formal period:** French Louisiana was effectively settled from ca. 1699. France ceded the western territory to Spain via the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762) and the eastern portion to Britain. Spain administered the western colony until 1800, when it was retroceded to France; the United States acquired the whole in the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718), seat of the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (France), then Spanish Louisiana (1769-1800), then briefly French again before U.S. acquisition.
- **Population during period:** Population data for the colonial period was not returned by available tools. French colonial censuses (recensements) survive and are described under Census Records below.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar), fur trade, maritime commerce. Enslaved labor was central under the Code Noir.
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers (including Canadians and Acadians after 1755), African-origin enslaved people, Native American populations, German settlers (German Coast, 1720s), Spanish settlers (post-1769), and free people of color.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism exclusively — legally mandated under both French and Spanish rule. No Protestant congregations were permitted.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Natchez Massacre (1729); Acadian deportation and Louisiana resettlement (1755-1785); Spanish takeover (1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary and jurisdictional changes

Three distinct administrations governed the 1700s:

1. **French Louisiana (1699-1769):** Records created by the Superior Council and Catholic parishes. The Superior Council held judicial, administrative, and notarial authority.
2. **Spanish Louisiana (1769-1800):** The Cabildo replaced the Superior Council. Catholic parish registers continued in parallel, now in Spanish.
3. **Brief French interval (1800-1803) and U.S. acquisition (1803):** Transition period; records are sparse.

Critical point: the effective administrative split is **1769**, not 1762 (when the treaty was signed). Records for a single family may span both series in the same parish and notarial archives.

The territory was enormous. Most surviving colonial records concern the lower Mississippi settlements (New Orleans, German Coast, Pointe Coupee, Natchitoches). The eastern portion — including Mobile — was ceded to Britain in 1763 and those records followed British colonial channels, not New Orleans repositories.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no civil registration during the French colonial period. The Catholic Church held exclusive authority over baptisms, marriages, and burials. The FamilySearch Louisiana Vital Records page did not return Louisiana-specific content, so no statewide civil registration start date can be confirmed from tool results for this era.
- **What exists:** Catholic sacramental registers are the functional vital records of the period. St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers surviving from 1720, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans); Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans; partially on FamilySearch (collection 1612905).
- **Gaps:** Records before 1720 are extremely sparse. Fires, floods, and deterioration damaged early registers.
- **Note:** The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, so sacramental registers are the principal source for enslaved ancestors — though entries are often brief (first name, owner's name, approximate age only).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholicism only (legally mandated).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages (including marriage contracts before a notary), burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral archives; Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans; Louisiana Historical Center; partially microfilmed and digitized by FamilySearch.
- **Language:** French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769), with Latin formulaic phrases throughout. Researchers must read the original languages.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection ID 1612905, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — approximately 987,654 records and 493,827 images.
- **Digitization level:** The two FamilySearch digitized volumes for this period (image group numbers 004330991 and 004330992) are **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only in French and Spanish.** See the repository guide below.

### Census records

- **French colonial censuses:** The French colonial government conducted periodic recensements beginning in the early 1700s. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for the colony, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **Spanish colonial censuses:** The Spanish administration also took periodic censuses after 1769.
- **U.S. federal census:** The first federal census covering Louisiana was 1810 — after the colonial period.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls at ANOM are largely physical only. Some have been transcribed and published in genealogical literature. No indexed online access is confirmed from tool results.

### Probate and court records (Superior Council / Cabildo)

- **Types:** Estate inventories, succession proceedings, guardianships, civil suits, land concessions, contracts. Under French and Spanish civil law, notarial acts are the primary vehicle for property transfers, marriage settlements, and estate dispositions — not a county court.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection 2078341 "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) covers part of the late French and all of the Spanish colonial period.
- **Superior Council records:** FamilySearch volume 004330992 — "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), 1699-1769" — 149 images, in French and Spanish, **0% indexed, browse-only.**
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans) holds Superior Council and Cabildo records; partially digitized.
- **Access note:** Records are in French (pre-1769) or Spanish (post-1769). Browsing requires reading 18th-century French or Spanish script.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** French and Spanish civil law traditions, not English common law. Land was granted as arpent-frontage lots along waterways — long and narrow, not rectangular survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French Crown concessions were granted by the Superior Council; Spanish grants by the Cabildo and Spanish Crown. These are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).
- **Notarial records:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Public access is available at that center.
- **Types:** Land grants (concessions), notarial property contracts, mortgage instruments, marriage settlements.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office (Baton Rouge); New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; Louisiana Historical Center; American State Papers (Public Lands — widely available in print and digitized).

### Notarial records (unique emphasis for Louisiana)

Louisiana's civil law tradition makes notarial archives far more central than in any common-law state. These are not supplementary sources — they are the primary source for wills, marriage settlements, property transactions, manumissions, apprenticeships, and contracts of all kinds.

- **Date range:** Surviving New Orleans notarial records begin in the 1730s.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (in-person; finding aids online); Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch Wiki search result identifies the Notarial Archives Research Center as providing public access ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** French-Indian wars, Natchez War (1729), Seven Years' War (ending 1763), American Revolution (Spain participated from Louisiana, 1779-1783).
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, officer commissions, troop rosters, and pension-like grants. French military records are held at the Archives de la Guerre (Vincennes, France). Spanish military records for Louisiana are in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) and Archivo General de Simancas.
- **Access:** No FamilySearch-indexed military collection for Louisiana's colonial period was returned by tool results. Largely physical only or requiring direct contact with French and Spanish national archives. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) covers military records generally but no Louisiana colonial-specific collection was identified.

### Cemetery records

- **Context:** Burials are recorded in Catholic parish registers (see Church Records). A separate cemetery-records administrative system did not exist during the French colonial period.
- **Major burial sites:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (New Orleans, established 1789, Spanish period); earlier burials in church grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) was returned by external links search as a general resource; colonial-era coverage is sparse.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper, the Moniteur de la Louisiane, began in 1794 (Spanish period, near the end of the colonial era). No newspapers existed for the earlier French period.
- **Content value:** Extremely limited for 1700-1762. The 1794-1803 interval has some coverage.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Library; Tulane University; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) — but colonial-era coverage is sparse.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant arrivals:** French settlers from France and Canada (1699-1769); German settlers (German Coast, ca. 1720s); Acadian refugees from Nova Scotia (1755-1785); enslaved Africans via the slave trade.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists; slave manifests; notarial indenture contracts; Superior Council admission records.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) holds French colonial ship records and emigrant lists, confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki results ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)). NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds some materials transferred at the Louisiana Purchase.
- **Passenger list note:** Colonial-era French passenger lists and emigrant contracts are in French; some have been transcribed in genealogical literature (e.g., Robichaux's Acadian publications). Examine full manifests when found — infants and children traveling with parents are listed.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Taille (head tax) and tithe records under French administration; Spanish-period tax records under the Cabildo.
- **Date range:** Sparse surviving records; most colonial tax documentation is embedded within Superior Council or Cabildo proceedings.
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center; ANOM (France).
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls partly function as population and property counts and can substitute for missing tax records.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (col. 1612905); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (col. 2078341); 2 digitized browse-only volumes (004330991, 004330992) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (post-colonial period only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal-era records post-1803; some colonial-era materials transferred at Purchase | Free to access; some records require request |
| Fold3 | Military records (general; no Louisiana colonial-specific collection confirmed) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (general; colonial-era coverage sparse) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (1794 onward; sparse for colonial era) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned exactly 2 digitized volumes covering this place and period (the complete set — no additional pages). Both are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; they must be browsed image by image in French and Spanish. The `collections_search` returned 4 total collections; the church (1612905) and probate (2078341) collections overlap the colonial period and are name-indexed at FamilySearch.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records (French, 1699-1769); Cabildo records (Spanish, 1769-1803); partially digitized | In-person; some materials online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s onward; oldest continuous notarial archive in North America | In-person; finding aids online |
| Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans | Original Catholic parish registers; sacramental records | In-person; contact archdiocese |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | State-era records; some colonial-era transferred materials | In-person; online catalog |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence; colonial census rolls; emigrant records | In-person or written request; partial digitization at archim.culture.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana (1769-1803) | In-person or written request; partial digitization at pares.mcu.es |
| Tulane University (Howard-Tilton Memorial Library) | Louisiana Historical Association collection; colonial-era manuscripts and publications | In-person; some online finding aids |

---

## Records NOT online

The following exist for the French colonial period but are not available in any indexed online database:

- Colonial census rolls (recensements) — held at ANOM, not indexed online
- French metropolitan military records — held at Archives de la Guerre (Vincennes) and Service Historique de la Defense
- Spanish military and administrative records for Louisiana — at Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Archivo General de Simancas; partial digitization at pares.mcu.es but not name-indexed for Louisiana specifically
- Ship passenger and emigrant contracts — at ANOM; some published transcriptions exist but no indexed online database
- Slave manifests and Code Noir baptismal entries in many original registers — unindexed even where images are online
- Natchitoches-area and upper-territory records — sparser, less often digitized

---

## Known record losses

- St. Louis Cathedral's earliest registers were damaged; surviving registers begin ca. 1720, not from the colony's founding.
- Some Superior Council records were damaged or lost during the turbulent administration transfers (French to Spanish, 1769; Spanish to French to U.S., 1800-1803).
- Records for Mobile and the eastern portion of French Louisiana, ceded to Britain in 1763, followed British colonial channels and are largely in British colonial archives or NARA — not the New Orleans repositories.
- Records for interior settlements (above Natchitoches) are fragmented and held across repositories on two continents.

---

## Research tips

- **Catholic parish is the genealogical jurisdiction, not any civil unit.** Under both French and Spanish rule, the parish — not a county or district court — created and held vital records. Identify which parish covered your ancestor's location before searching. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

- **Records are in French and Spanish, not English.** Both digitized FamilySearch volumes (004330991 and 004330992) are 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, and in 18th-century French and Spanish script. Browsing them requires reading the original language.

- **Notarial archives are essential, not supplementary.** Louisiana's civil law tradition means wills, marriage settlements, property transactions, and manumissions were executed before a notary — not filed in a county probate court. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center is the functional equivalent of a county courthouse for this period. ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))

- **Search both French and Spanish series.** A family present before 1769 appears in French records; their descendants appear in Spanish records. The split is 1769 (effective Spanish administration), not 1762.

- **Acadian ancestry:** If your ancestors were Acadian refugees (arrived 1755-1785), ANOM (France) and published Acadian-specific indexes are essential alongside Louisiana parish registers. Robichaux's published works contain transcribed records.

- **Code Noir and enslaved ancestors:** Sacramental registers are the primary — sometimes only — record of enslaved individuals. Manumission documents are in the notarial archives.

- **American State Papers (Public Lands):** For land claims confirmed after the Louisiana Purchase, this series documents colonial-era grants and their U.S. confirmation. Widely available in print and digitized.

- **Published genealogical literature:** Given the difficulty of accessing original records, major published works (Winston De Ville's colonial Louisiana genealogies, Robichaux's Acadian publications) contain transcriptions and abstracts of records. Consult WorldCat or Tulane's library before traveling to archives.

- **Do not assume no record means no record.** The two FamilySearch volumes for this period contain 413 combined images of unindexed records. A name search returning nothing does not mean the person is absent — the records must be browsed directly.

---

The guide has been saved to the project as `loc_001` in `research.json`.

---

French colonial Louisiana (roughly 1700-1803) left behind an unusually rich but dispersed paper trail. The Catholic Church kept the only vital records — baptisms, marriages, and burials — because it was the sole legally recognized church under both French and Spanish rule. Those registers, plus the notarial archives in New Orleans (wills, property contracts, marriage settlements), are the backbone of any family search for this period. Nearly everything is in French or Spanish, and most digitized records on FamilySearch must be browsed image by image — name searching will miss them. The most important physical repositories are in New Orleans (the Louisiana Historical Center and Notarial Archives Research Center), but French metropolitan records (at ANOM in Aix-en-Provence) and Spanish colonial records (at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville) are often essential for tracing families back to their European origins or for military and administrative records.

If you have a specific parish, family name, or research question in mind, the next step is building a research plan targeting the record types most likely to contain that family — starting with the St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers and the notarial archives for the New Orleans area, or the appropriate regional parish for settlements outside the city.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formal period:** French Louisiana existed from 1682; effective settlement began ca. 1699. France ceded the western territory to Spain via the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), and the eastern portion to Britain. Spain administered the western colony until 1800, when it was retroceded to France; the United States acquired it in the Louisiana Purchase (1803).
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718), seat of the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Colony of New France (France), then Spanish Louisiana (1769-1800), then briefly French again before U.S. acquisition.
- **Population during period:** Population data for the colonial period was not returned by the tools. French censuses and census-like rolls survive and are described under Census Records.
- **Economy:** Plantation agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar), fur trade, maritime commerce. Enslaved labor was central under the Code Noir.
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers (including Canadians and Acadians after 1755), African-origin enslaved people, Native American populations, German settlers (German Coast, 1720s), Spanish settlers (post-1769), and free people of color.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholicism exclusively (legally mandated under both French and Spanish rule).
- **Key historical events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Natchez Massacre (1729); Acadian deportation and resettlement (1755-1785); Spanish takeover (1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary and jurisdictional changes
Three distinct administrations during the 1700s: French Louisiana (1699-1769), Spanish Louisiana (1769-1800), brief French interval (1800-1803). Records for a single family may span all three in the same parish registers and notarial archives. The effective split date for French vs. Spanish records is 1769, not 1762.

## Available record types

### Vital records
No civil registration existed during the French colonial period. Catholic sacramental registers are the functional vital records. St. Louis Cathedral registers survive from 1720. FamilySearch collection 1612905 covers 1718-1925 with ~987,654 records and 493,827 images.

### Church records
Roman Catholicism only. Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Records in French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769). Held at the Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, Louisiana Historical Center, and partially on FamilySearch. Two digitized volumes on FamilySearch (image groups 004330991 and 004330992) are browse-only, 0% indexed, in French and Spanish.

### Census records
French colonial recensements and Spanish colonial censuses exist but are largely at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence, France). Not available in an indexed online database. U.S. federal census begins 1810, post-colonial period.

### Probate and court records
FamilySearch collection 2078341 (Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984). Superior Council records (1699-1769) are at the Louisiana Historical Center, partially digitized as image group 004330992 (149 images, browse-only, French/Spanish). Spanish Cabildo records continue the series post-1769.

### Land records
French arpent-lot system along waterways. Concessions via Superior Council (French) and Cabildo (Spanish). American State Papers: Public Lands documents colonial grants confirmed post-Purchase. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds notarial property records from 1730s onward.

### Notarial records
Central to Louisiana research due to civil law tradition. Contain wills, marriage settlements, property sales, manumissions, contracts. New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access. Records from 1730s onward.

### Military records
French military records at Archives de la Guerre (Vincennes, France); Spanish military records at Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and Archivo General de Simancas. No FamilySearch-indexed colonial Louisiana military collection identified.

### Cemetery records
Burials recorded in Catholic parish registers. St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 established 1789. FindAGrave (findagrave.com) available but colonial-era coverage sparse.

### Newspaper records
First Louisiana newspaper (Moniteur de la Louisiane) begun 1794. No newspapers existed for the French period (pre-1762).

### Immigration records
French colonial emigrant contracts and ship lists at ANOM (France). Acadian resettlement records in ANOM and published indexes. Slave manifests and Code Noir baptismal entries in sacramental registers.

### Tax records
Taille and tithe records embedded in Superior Council/Cabildo proceedings. Colonial census rolls partly function as property counts. Held at Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1718-1925 (col. 1612905); Probate Records 1756-1984 (col. 2078341); 2 browse-only digitized volumes | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal-era records; some colonial-era materials | Free/request |
| Fold3 | Military records (general) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (sparse for colonial era) | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans) | Superior Council and Cabildo records; partially digitized | In-person; some online |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s; oldest continuous notarial office in North America | In-person; finding aids online |
| Archives of the Archdiocese of New Orleans | Catholic parish registers | In-person; contact archdiocese |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | State-era and some colonial-era materials | In-person; online catalog |
| ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records; census rolls; emigrant records | In-person or written request; partial digitization at archim.culture.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial administrative records (1769-1803) | In-person or written request; partial digitization at pares.mcu.es |
| Tulane University (Howard-Tilton Library) | Louisiana Historical Association collection; colonial manuscripts | In-person; some online finding aids |

## Records NOT online
- Colonial census rolls (at ANOM)
- French military records (Archives de la Guerre, Vincennes)
- Spanish military and administrative records (Archivo General de Indias, Seville)
- Ship passenger and emigrant contracts (ANOM)
- Most Natchitoches-area and upper-territory records

## Known record losses
- St. Louis Cathedral early registers damaged; surviving registers begin ca. 1720
- Some Superior Council records lost or damaged during administration transfers (1769; 1800-1803)
- Mobile and eastern French Louisiana ceded to Britain 1763; those records are in British colonial archives or NARA, not New Orleans repositories

## Research tips
- Catholic parish is the genealogical jurisdiction, not any civil unit. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- All colonial records are in French or Spanish — browsing the unindexed volumes requires ability to read 18th-century French and Spanish script
- Notarial archives are essential for wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- Search both French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769) series for any family with records spanning 1769
- Code Noir entries in sacramental registers are the primary source for enslaved ancestors
- American State Papers: Public Lands documents colonial land grants confirmed post-Purchase
- Published genealogical literature (De Ville, Robichaux) contains transcriptions of hard-to-access colonial records

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Mining Region (Late 1800s)

This guide focuses on Schuylkill County (Pottsville), with notes for the broader anthracite region: Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties.

---

## Critical Jurisdictional Note

**Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878** — it was carved from Luzerne County. Any event in the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 belongs in Luzerne County records. Searching only Lackawanna for that era will miss everything.

---

## Key Records by Type

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide birth/death registration until **1906** — so civil vital records largely don't exist for this period. County marriage registration began in **1885**.
- FamilySearch: [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) — 524,000+ indexed records
- **Substitute for births/deaths:** Church records (see below)

---

### Church Records ← Most Important Source
Ethnic national parishes are the key. A Polish miner in Mahanoy City attended a completely different parish than his Irish neighbor — each has a separate register.

- **Irish/Welsh miners (1840s–60s):** Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Welsh Baptist, Methodist Episcopal
- **Eastern European miners (1880s+):** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Ukrainian, Italian national parishes; Eastern Rite churches
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, burial, confirmation
- **FamilySearch:** [Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records, 1708–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/...) — 1.2 million records, indexed with images
- **Physical:** Diocese of Scranton and Diocese of Allentown archives for undigitized registers

---

### Federal Census Records
- 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 (the **1890 census was destroyed by fire** — a hard gap)
- **1880 onward:** Lists relationship to head of household
- **1900:** Lists birth month/year and years in the US — invaluable for immigrant miners
- **Mortality schedules** (1850–1880): Lists persons who died in the preceding year — a substitute death record
- Available on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free)

---

### Mining Company & Occupational Records ← Unique to This Region
| Record | Coverage | FamilySearch Volume | Index Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mine Worker Employment Cards | Schuylkill Co., 1870–1900 | 002240015 (410 images) | 95% name-indexed ✓ |
| Mine Accident Reports | Luzerne Co., 1870–1895 | 002240016 (287 images) | Browse-only |
| Colliery Payroll Ledgers | Lackawanna Co., 1878–1900 | 002240017 (199 images) | Browse-only |

- **State Mine Inspector Reports (annual, from 1870):** List fatal accidents by name, age, nationality, cause of death — may be the only pre-1906 death record for miners killed on the job. Held at Pennsylvania State Archives
- **UMWA records (from 1890):** Membership rolls and grievance files at UMWA archives and Historical Society of Schuylkill County
- Note: 23 total digitized volumes exist for this region — only 3 are detailed above; browse FamilySearch for the remainder

---

### Probate & Court Records
- **Probate:** FamilySearch collection 1999196, "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" — 3.2 million images, browse-only (no name index)
- **Naturalizations (pre-1906):** Filed in any county court. Schuylkill County naturalizations 1840s–1906 are at the Pennsylvania State Archives. Miners often filed the declaration in one county and the petition in another if they moved

---

### Immigration Records
Many miners entered through Philadelphia or New York (Castle Garden to 1892, Ellis Island from 1892).
- **1895+ passenger manifests** list the immigrant's last home address and a US contact — directly useful for tracing origins
- Indexed on Ancestry (subscription), FamilySearch (free)
- NARA holds original pension and naturalization files

---

### Newspapers ← Strong Substitute for Death Records
The **Miners' Journal (Pottsville)** is the paper of record for Schuylkill County. For accident deaths before 1906, it often named the deceased, gave age and nationality, listed surviving family, and identified the mine.
- Newspapers.com (subscription) has digitized Pennsylvania papers
- Ethnic-language papers (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak) from the 1880s are largely microfilm-only at the Pennsylvania State Library or local historical societies

---

### Cemetery Records
- FindAGrave has substantial Pennsylvania coverage
- Sexton records and burial registers held by individual parishes or diocesan archives

---

### Tax & Land Records
- **Tax lists** can place a miner in a township in years between censuses
- **Deed records** may be absent — many miners rented company housing in patch towns and never owned land
- Schuylkill County Courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives hold these

---

## Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | State Mine Inspector reports; Schuylkill Co. naturalizations 1840s–1906; state land/warrant/survey records | In-person; some mail requests |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local mining records, UMWA materials, newspapers, local histories | In-person |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton) | Mining community records, oral histories, company records | In-person |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish registers (Lackawanna/Luzerne area) | Written inquiry |
| **Diocese of Allentown Archives** | Catholic parish registers (Schuylkill/Carbon area) | Written inquiry |
| **FamilySearch** | Church records, census, marriages, mine employment cards | Free |
| **Ancestry** | Census, passenger lists, newspapers | Subscription |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Identify the ethnic parish first.** Nationality + religion + specific patch town → specific parish register. This is the most important step.
2. **Start with Mine Worker Employment Cards (vol. 002240015)** — 95% indexed, covers 1870–1900 Schuylkill Co.
3. **Use the 1900 census** as your best tool for immigrant miners — it gives years in the US and birth month/year.
4. **Miners' Journal** for any mine accident death before 1906 — it's often the only record naming the deceased.
5. **Lackawanna before 1878 = Luzerne County records.** Don't forget this.
6. **Company towns were unincorporated** — no municipal vital records. Church + county court are your only options.
7. **Immigrant sequence:** Many men came alone, naturalized, then sent for their families. Search passenger lists for the wife and children arriving later — the 1895+ manifests give the US contact address, which can confirm the miner's location.

---

The backbone of research here is **census + church records + mine employment/accident records**, supplemented by naturalization records and passenger lists for immigrant origins. The absence of civil vital records before 1906 is the defining challenge of this region and time period — but the ethnic parish registers and mine-specific occupational records more than compensate when found.
